transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. What brings you to see me today?

Well, hi. Thank you for seeing me. Honestly, it’s... it’s my job that finally pushed me to make the appointment. I mean, the main thing that brings me in is that I just cannot keep my mind on a single task long enough to actually finish it anymore. And it doesn't even matter how important it is, or how much trouble I'll be in if I don't get it done. 

I'm a computer support specialist, so my whole day is basically troubleshooting, right? Getting to the bottom of things. But I'll be sitting at my desk—like, just the other day, I had to trace this really urgent network problem for one of our main clients. Their whole system was bottlenecking, it was a huge deal. So I pull up the server logs, which I've done a million times, and I start reading. But then, I don't know, maybe ten minutes later I'll suddenly snap to and realize I've just reread the exact same block of log entries three times in a row. Three times! And I still have absolutely no idea what they actually say. 

It's like my eyes are moving across the screen, but my brain is just entirely disconnected from the process. It's incredibly frustrating because I know the stakes are high, the client is waiting, my boss is waiting, but I just sit there staring at the text and nothing goes in. I used to be able to just power through it, get a cup of coffee and force myself to focus, but now it's happening all day long. Every time I sit down to do something, I just can't seem to stay locked in long enough to get to the end of it.
Did you experience similar problems with attention and focus when you were growing up, like during your school years?

Oh, absolutely. It’s... well, it’s funny you ask that, because I've actually been thinking a lot about my childhood lately, especially with how bad things have gotten at work. You look back and try to figure out when things started falling apart, but the truth is, I think it was always like this. 

I mean, my mother—she’s 82 now, living down in Florida—she still jokes about it to this day whenever we talk on the phone. She actually kept all my old grade school report cards in this big plastic tub, and she loves reminding me about what the teachers used to write. It was always the exact same story, year after year. They would write that I was a bright kid, that I had a lot of potential, but... well, they said I never, ever stayed in my seat. I was always up and wandering around the classroom, checking out the pencil sharpener or whatever. 

And they’d get so frustrated because I would just blurt out the answers. Like, the teacher would be halfway through asking a question and I’d just shout it out without raising my hand. I just couldn't hold it in, it was like this physical pressure. And the homework... oh man. My mother would sit with me at the kitchen table, make sure I did every single math problem, put it in my folder, and then somehow, between the front door and my desk at school, it would just vanish. I lost my homework all the time, even when I had literally just done it the night before and knew exactly what the answers were. 

So, yeah, I guess the signs were all there. I think maybe because I got good grades on the tests, they just thought I was a difficult boy, or just overly energetic, which is what they tended to call it back in the seventies. But it was always a huge struggle, even back then, just trying to sit still and do what I was supposed to do without making a complete mess of the routine...
Nowadays as an adult, do you still feel physically restless or have trouble sitting still?

Oh, god, yes. It never really went away, it just... changed shape, I guess? Like, I'm not running around the classroom checking the pencil sharpener anymore, obviously, but the internal feeling is still exactly the same. 

It's like... even when I'm supposed to just sit still and listen, like in a staff meeting or when a client is explaining a complicated issue on a conference call, it feels like there's this actual motor humming right under my skin. Just this constant, vibrating energy. I'll be sitting in one of those awful ergonomic chairs they bought us last year—which, by the way, are supposed to be so comfortable but I find them completely suffocating—and my boss will be going over the quarterly security protocols. And I know I need to listen, I know it's important, but my leg will just start bouncing. It bounces so much the whole conference table shakes sometimes. 

And inside, my brain is just screaming that I need to stand up, or I need to go check on a server rack, or just... move on to the next problem right that exact second. It’s exhausting, really. I end up shifting my weight a hundred times, crossing and uncrossing my legs, tapping my pen until someone glares at me. My coworkers probably think I drink way too much coffee, which, I mean, I do, but that’s not what’s causing this. It’s just this intense, physical urge that builds up in my chest and my arms. 

Sometimes I actually have to fake a cough and excuse myself to go to the bathroom just so I can pace the hallway for two minutes. Because if I don't get up and walk it off, I feel like I'm going to jump out of my own skin. And you'd think at 53 years old I'd have figured out how to just sit in a chair for a one-hour meeting, but it honestly feels harder now than it ever did. I just... I can't settle. I'm always on edge, physically, just waiting for the split second I'm allowed to stand up again.
